Implementation Methodologies for Specialist Systems

Introduction

Yes, many specialist systems have distinct implementation methodologies.

In practice, these methodologies usually come from one of four sources:

  • vendor-branded methodologies
  • systems integrator or partner delivery frameworks
  • industry-specific engineering or validation lifecycles
  • generic project delivery models tailored to the platform, such as agile, waterfall, hybrid, or phased rollout

Some products have a very explicit named methodology, while others rely on a delivery pattern shaped by the operational and regulatory context.

Key Principle

The implementation approach usually depends less on the software brand alone and more on the type of system being deployed.

For example:

  • a large ERP platform is usually implemented through a fit-to-standard, configuration-led method
  • an industrial control system is usually implemented through an engineering lifecycle with testing and commissioning
  • a healthcare or laboratory platform often requires a validation-heavy rollout
  • a multi-site retail or operational platform often uses a template-and-wave rollout

Named Vendor Methodologies

SAP

SAP historically used ASAP, while its current implementation method is SAP Activate.

SAP describes SAP Activate as a structured implementation framework combining best practices, implementation methodology, and guided configuration tools. SAP also describes six phases in the framework and positions it around fit-to-standard and clean core principles.[@sap_activate]

Oracle

Oracle has long used the Oracle Unified Method (OUM) as its formal delivery method framework. Oracle continues to maintain OUM learning and training content, including structure, principles, and delivery readiness material.[@oracle_oum]

In practice, Oracle projects may also use cloud-specific implementation approaches layered on top of OUM or aligned with product-specific delivery guidance.[@oracle_oum_training]

Guidewire

Guidewire refers to SurePath as a guided, proven implementation approach intended to support faster and more predictable delivery. This is especially relevant in InsuranceSuite and cloud-oriented implementations, often alongside agile delivery and partner-led execution.[@guidewire_surepath; @guidewire_training]

Systems Without a Single Public Branded Method

Not every specialist platform has a widely publicised branded method.

Many sectors instead rely on a delivery model shaped by operational realities:

  • industrial and OT platforms tend to use detailed engineering, FAT, SAT, commissioning, and handover
  • clinical and regulated systems tend to use controlled deployment, traceability, validation, and strong change management
  • transport, hospitality, retail, and logistics systems often use site templates and deployment waves
  • core banking and insurance systems often combine vendor guidance, systems integrator methods, and programme-level governance

Methodology Styles by System Category

System Category Typical Delivery Style Common Characteristics Named Examples
ERP and enterprise platforms Fit-to-standard, configuration-led, agile or hybrid Process design, configuration, extensions, data migration, integration, testing, training, cutover SAP Activate, Oracle Unified Method
Insurance platforms Agile, configuration-led, partner-led Product configuration, integration, data conversion, iterative releases, business readiness Guidewire SurePath
Core banking platforms Package-led transformation Product fit-gap, process standardisation, data migration, controls, phased migration Vendor + SI methodologies
Industrial control systems Engineering lifecycle / V-model Requirements, control philosophy, detailed design, FAT, SAT, commissioning, handover Vendor engineering methods
MES / OT manufacturing platforms Hybrid engineering + operational rollout Solution design, shop-floor integration, testing, commissioning, training, stabilisation Vendor / partner methods
Healthcare and laboratory systems Validation-heavy phased rollout Workflow design, controlled configuration, data migration, validation, training, go-live support Vendor + clinical transformation methods
Retail, hospitality, POS, WMS, TMS Template-based rollout Core template, localisation, pilot, wave deployment, site readiness, cutover Vendor / partner rollout methods
Airport, airline, rail, and transport systems Programme-based operational deployment Integration-heavy planning, operational rehearsal, training, cutover, resilience testing Vendor + operational change methods

Typical Phases by Methodology Type

1. Configuration-Led Business Platform Method

Typical for:

  • SAP
  • Oracle ERP
  • Guidewire
  • core banking
  • insurance policy administration
  • WMS and TMS platforms

Typical phases:

  1. mobilisation
  2. discovery and fit-to-standard
  3. solution design
  4. configuration and extension
  5. data migration and integration
  6. testing
  7. training and business readiness
  8. cutover
  9. hypercare and transition to support

2. Engineering and Commissioning Method

Typical for:

  • SCADA
  • DCS
  • plant automation
  • utility control platforms
  • some MES deployments

Typical phases:

  1. requirements and control philosophy
  2. architecture and security design
  3. detailed engineering
  4. build and integration
  5. factory acceptance testing
  6. site acceptance testing
  7. commissioning
  8. operational handover
  9. optimisation and support

3. Validation-Heavy Regulated Deployment Method

Typical for:

  • EHR / EMR
  • PACS
  • LIS / LIMS
  • CTMS
  • regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing systems

Typical phases:

  1. process and workflow assessment
  2. requirements and traceability
  3. controlled configuration
  4. validation planning
  5. data migration and interface testing
  6. user acceptance and validation evidence
  7. training and readiness
  8. go-live control
  9. stabilisation and audit support

4. Template and Wave Rollout Method

Typical for:

  • POS
  • hotel PMS
  • SIS
  • WMS across multiple sites
  • restaurant platforms
  • branch or regional operational systems

Typical phases:

  1. define core template
  2. pilot implementation
  3. localisation and site readiness
  4. data and integration preparation
  5. cutover by wave
  6. post-go-live support
  7. rollout governance and lessons learned

Why Methodology Choice Matters

Choosing the wrong implementation methodology creates major delivery risk.

A methodology should match:

  • the criticality of the platform
  • the degree of regulation
  • the level of standardisation versus customisation
  • the number of deployment sites
  • the data migration complexity
  • the integration footprint
  • the need for operational rehearsal, commissioning, or validation

For example, a SCADA deployment should not be run exactly like a SaaS HR implementation, and a hospital EHR rollout should not be treated as a simple packaged software installation.

Practical Architecture View

A useful architecture classification is:

System Type Best-Fit Methodology Logic
Transaction-heavy business platform Fit-to-standard, process-led, configuration-first
Operational control platform Engineering-led, safety-aware, commissioning-based
Regulated record platform Validation-heavy, traceable, readiness-led
Multi-site operational platform Template-based, pilot-first, wave rollout
Highly integrated legacy transformation Hybrid programme method with phased coexistence

Enterprise Governance Implications

Implementation methodology should be aligned with governance disciplines such as:

  • programme and project management
  • architecture governance
  • cyber security and resilience
  • data migration governance
  • test management
  • operational readiness
  • training and change management
  • service transition and support model design

This means implementation methodology is not just a project method; it is also a governance and assurance mechanism.

Conclusion

Yes, there are specific methodologies for implementing specialist systems.

Some are explicitly branded, such as:

  • SAP Activate
  • Oracle Unified Method
  • Guidewire SurePath

Others are not branded in the same way, but still follow recognisable industry-specific patterns such as:

  • engineering and commissioning lifecycles
  • validation-heavy regulated deployment
  • template-and-wave rollouts
  • package-led transformation methods

The most useful way to analyse them is not only by vendor, but by system class, risk profile, regulatory burden, and deployment model.
